Multimodal Deep Learning for Radiologic Breast Cancer Triage

Multimodal Radiologic Breast Cancer Triage Using Graph-Infused Transformers: A Controlled Multi-Phase Evaluation and Reproducibility Audit

Authors: Antigravity AI Research Consortium
Date: October 16, 2026
Repository & Artifact Archive: c:\Users\admin\Music\Breast Cancer1
Execution Context: Final Consolidated Research Manuscript (Phase D9)
Correspondence: AI Medical Imaging Research Division

Abstract

Automated radiologic breast cancer triage offers substantial potential to optimize screening workflows by expediting review of suspicious lesions while reducing false alarms in routine examinations. However, clinical adoption requires rigorous validation, leak-free patient-level data partitioning, and honest reporting of statistical uncertainty. In this study, we present a comprehensive, multi-phase investigation of a Multimodal Graph-Infused Transformer (GIT) architecture evaluated on the Breast Cancer Multimodal Imaging Dataset (BCMID), comprising paired digital mammography and ultrasound examinations.

The architecture leverages frozen unimodal feature representations pre-extracted from an EfficientNet-B0 mammogram backbone (1280-dim) and a Vision Transformer (ViT-B/16) ultrasound backbone (768-dim), dynamically fused through a side-aware Graph Attention Network (GAT) and a multi-head cross-attention Transformer. Following systematic exploration of class-balanced focal loss (γ = 1.5, α = [1.0, 5.1111]) to address severe class imbalance (5.1 : 1 negative-to-positive ratio), Candidate C3 was established as the primary benchmark. A controlled hyperparameter exploration on validation data selected Candidate D5 (halved learning rate lr = 5 × 10 − 5) based on validation sensitivity gains (87.50% vs. 75.00%,  + 1 patient detected).

Following upstream development and quarantine during Phase D1–D7, the 47-patient held-out test cohort (Npos = 7, Nneg = 40) was unblinded once for a locked evaluation at the canonical operating threshold τ = 0.50. On held-out test data, both models achieved identical cancer detection yield (85.71% sensitivity, 6 of 7 suspicious/actionable cases triaged, missing the exact same BI-RADS 5 patient). However, Candidate D5 misclassified two additional benign patients as suspicious, resulting in lower specificity (80.00% vs. 85.00%, 8 vs. 6 false positives), accuracy (80.85% vs. 85.11%), precision (42.86% vs. 50.00%), F1-score (0.5714 vs. 0.6316), and ROC-AUC (0.8964 vs. 0.9036). A paired McNemar exact test confirmed statistical equivalence (p = 0.5000, 95.74% classification agreement).

Due to the limited test cohort size (N = 47) and small positive sample size (Npos = 7), the 95% Clopper-Pearson exact confidence interval [21] for sensitivity spans from 42.13% to 99.64%. We provide a complete forensic reconciliation of historical metrics, transparently resolving earlier transcription discrepancies. We conclude that Candidate C3 remains the preferred reference benchmark, but emphasize that these results represent internal retrospective proof-of-concept evidence rather than definitive clinical diagnostic validation.

Keywords

Radiologic Breast Triage, Multimodal Deep Learning, Graph Attention Networks, Cross-Modal Transformers, Class-Balanced Focal Loss, BCMID Dataset, Decision Calibration, Scientific Reproducibility.

1. Introduction

Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy and a leading cause of cancer mortality among women worldwide [1, 2]. Population-based mammographic screening programs have successfully reduced disease-specific mortality through early detection. However, standard two-dimensional full-field digital mammography (FFDM) suffers from well-documented diagnostic limitations, particularly in women with dense fibroglandular breast tissue, where overlapping dense tissue frequently obscures malignant lesions (the “masking effect”), leading to reduced sensitivity [3]. Complementary automated breast ultrasound (US) significantly enhances cancer detection in dense breasts, yet manual sonographic interpretation is time-consuming, highly operator-dependent, and prone to high false-positive rates that induce unnecessary tissue biopsies and substantial patient anxiety [3].

Automated radiologic triage offers a compelling technical solution to this clinical dilemma. Rather than attempting to establish an autonomous pathology diagnosis, a radiologic triage system classifies multi-view screening examinations into two operational categories: 1. Low-Risk Screening (LOW_RISK): Examinations categorized as BI-RADS (Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System) Categories 1 (negative), 2 (benign findings), or 3 (probably benign findings requiring routine interval screening), which can be safely cleared through standard workflows. 2. Suspicious / Actionable Screening (SUSPICIOUS_ACTIONABLE): Examinations categorized as BI-RADS Categories 4A, 4B, 4C (suspicious abnormality), 5 (highly suggestive of malignancy), or 6 (known biopsy-proven malignancy), which demand urgent prioritized radiologist review and diagnostic tissue biopsy.

Despite the proliferation of deep learning models in medical imaging, widespread clinical translation has been hindered by severe methodological vulnerabilities. Published literature frequently exhibits data leakage across patient visits, lack of patient-level split stratification, over-reliance on overall accuracy in imbalanced cohorts, and post-hoc threshold optimization that artificially inflates test-set metrics [4, 5].

To address these challenges, this study presents a rigorous, fully auditable investigation of multimodal graph-and-transformer fusion using the Breast Cancer Multimodal Imaging Dataset (BCMID) [6]. We enforce strict methodological principles: - Complete root-patient split stratification with zero leakage across partitions. - Complete isolation of the held-out test cohort throughout all model development, loss modulation, hyperparameter tuning, and threshold calibration phases. - Transparent reporting of point metrics alongside exact counts, fractions, Wilson score intervals [22], Clopper-Pearson exact binomial bounds [21], and stratified bootstrap distributions. - A forensic audit reconciling historical metric discrepancies across prior project phases.

2. Related Work

2.1 Multimodal Fusion in Breast Imaging

Combining digital mammography and ultrasound has been extensively demonstrated to increase diagnostic sensitivity, particularly for occult lesions in dense breasts [3]. Early computational approaches relied on late fusion, averaging predicted probabilities from independent convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [7]. More recent architectures explore cross-attention mechanisms, where feature tokens from mammographic projections query sonographic feature maps [8]. However, standard attention mechanisms often ignore spatial and anatomical relationships between views (e.g., matching ipsilateral craniocaudal [CC] and mediolateral oblique [MLO] mammographic projections with targeted ipsilateral ultrasound sweeps).

2.2 Graph Neural Networks in Medical Computer Vision

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), and specifically Graph Attention Networks (GATs) [9], provide a mathematically principled framework for modeling non-Euclidean relational inductive biases. In multi-view medical imaging, individual images can be treated as graph nodes, while edges represent anatomical side relationships (ipsilateral vs. contralateral) or lesion proximities. Incorporating anatomical side embeddings into graph attention layers enables the network to aggregate multi-view evidence adaptively while penalizing discordant contralateral features.

2.3 Class Imbalance & Focal Modulation

Breast cancer screening populations are heavily dominated by normal and benign examinations, typically resulting in negative-to-positive ratios exceeding 5 : 1 in clinical cohorts [10]. Standard binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss tends to produce trivial majority-class classifiers that achieve high accuracy while failing to detect positive malignancies. While weighted BCE addresses marginal class frequencies, it treats easy and difficult samples identically. Focal loss, introduced by Lin et al. [11] and extended by Cui et al. [12], down-weights the gradient contribution of well-classified easy negative examples via a focusing parameter γ, forcing the network to concentrate gradients on hard, ambiguous borderline cases.

2.4 Probability Calibration in Clinical AI

A model with high discriminative ability (ROC-AUC) can nevertheless be dangerously miscalibrated if its predicted probabilities do not correspond to true empirical risks [13]. In clinical triage, poorly calibrated probabilities distort threshold selection and erode clinician trust. Brier score [14] and Expected Calibration Error (ECE) [13] serve as essential evaluation dimensions alongside discrete diagnostic classification metrics.

3. Dataset, Label Semantics & Patient-Level Splitting

3.1 The BCMID Cohort

The Breast Cancer Multimodal Imaging Dataset (BCMID) is a pioneering medical imaging repository collected retrospectively from Ayady Almostakbal Hospital in Alexandria, Egypt, between 2019 and 2022, and hosted on Zenodo (Record 15546909) [6]. The dataset provides paired multimodal imaging examinations—digital mammograms (CC and MLO views) and targeted ultrasound sweeps—alongside structured radiological reports and BI-RADS diagnostic assessments.

3.2 Label Definitions & Semantics

Radiological findings were mapped to standard American College of Radiology (ACR) BI-RADS assessment categories [2]: - Class 0 (LOW_RISK): BI-RADS 1 (negative), BI-RADS 2 (benign findings, e.g., simple cysts, benign calcifications), and BI-RADS 3 (probably benign findings). These cases represent routine screening examinations that require routine annual screening or short-term imaging follow-up. - Class 1 (SUSPICIOUS_ACTIONABLE): BI-RADS 4A, 4B, 4C (suspicious abnormalities requiring tissue biopsy), BI-RADS 5 (highly suggestive of malignancy, risk  > 95%), and BI-RADS 6 (biopsy-proven malignancy).

3.3 Patient-Level Stratified Partitioning

To guarantee zero data contamination across examinations, splitting was performed strictly at the biological root-patient level (root_patient_id), ensuring that multi-folder examinations from the same patient remained confined within the same split:

The four repeat-visit root patients were distributed such that Multi-Visit Patient Groups R1, R2, and R3 (6 folders) reside exclusively in Training, while Group R4 (2 folders) resides exclusively in Validation. The held-out test cohort contains zero repeat visits, representing 47 completely unique biological subjects. Partition intersections are strictly null (Train ∩ Val = ∅, Train ∩ Test = ∅, Val ∩ Test = ∅).

4. Proposed Methodology: Multimodal Graph-Infused Transformer (GIT)

The implemented pipeline combines frozen unimodal vision encoders with an expressive graph attention and cross-modal Transformer architecture, depicted in Figure 2:

Figure 2: Multimodal Graph-Infused Transformer (GIT) Architecture for Radiologic Breast Triage.

4.1 Frozen Feature Extraction

To ensure computational efficiency and avoid catastrophic forgetting on limited data, vision encoders were pre-trained on unimodal tasks and frozen: 1. Mammogram Feature Encoder (EMG): An EfficientNet-B0 backbone [15] pre-trained on mammographic images, extracting a 1280-dimensional feature vector per view (fMG ∈ ℝ1280). 2. Ultrasound Feature Encoder (EUS): A Vision Transformer (ViT-B/16) backbone [16] pre-trained on sonographic images, extracting a 768-dimensional feature vector per view (fUS ∈ ℝ768).

Features were pre-extracted into a locked binary cache data/features/patient_multimodal_features.pt under torch.no_grad().

4.2 Side-Aware Graph Attention Layer (GAT)

For a patient with M mammogram views and U ultrasound views, input features are projected into a shared hidden dimension d = 256: hi(0) = Wprojfi + eside(i) where eside(i) ∈ ℝ256 is a learnable anatomical side embedding representing Left (“L”), Right (“R”), Bilateral (“BIL”), or Unknown (“UNK”).

A 2-layer Graph Attention Network with 4 attention heads [9] processes inter-view relationships: $$\alpha_{ij} = \frac{\exp\left(\text{LeakyReLU}\left(\mathbf{a}^\top [\mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_i \parallel \mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_j \parallel \mathbf{e}_{\text{rel}(i,j)}]\right)\right)}{\sum_{k \in \mathcal{N}_i} \exp\left(\text{LeakyReLU}\left(\mathbf{a}^\top [\mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_i \parallel \mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_k \parallel \mathbf{e}_{\text{rel}(i,k)}]\right)\right)}$$ hi(l + 1) = σ(∑j ∈ 𝒩iαijW(l)hj(l)) This enables the network to exchange contextual information across views while explicitly incorporating ipsilateral alignment.

4.3 Multimodal Cross-Attention Transformer

The refined view representations are passed through a 2-layer Cross-Attention Transformer (8 attention heads, feedforward dimension dff = 1024, dropout rate 0.30) [17]. Dynamic padding masks MMG and MUS handle variable numbers of views across patients, ensuring that padded positions do not contribute to attention softmax distributions. Patient-level pooling yields a unified 256-dimensional multimodal embedding vector zpatient.

4.4 Class-Balanced Focal Loss Formulation

To counteract the 5.11 : 1 class imbalance without destabilizing gradients, we implemented Class-Balanced Focal Loss [11, 12]: FL(pt) =  − αt(1 − pt)γlog (pt) where pt is the model’s estimated probability for the true class, γ = 1.5 is the focusing exponent, and class weights are set to the inverse class frequencies normalized to the majority class: α = [1.0000, 5.1111]. The loss is normalized across each batch by dividing by the sum of sample weights: $$\mathcal{L} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^B \text{FL}(p_{t,i})}{\sum_{i=1}^B \alpha_{y_i}}$$

5. Experimental Setup & Predeclared Evaluation Protocol

5.1 Optimization Hyperparameters

  • Optimizer: AdamW (β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999, weight decay 0.01) [18].
  • Learning Rate Schedule: CosineAnnealingLR (Tmax = 20, ηmin = 10 − 6).
  • Batch Management: Physical batch size 8 with 2 gradient accumulation steps (effective batch size 16).
  • Mixed Precision: PyTorch Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) autocasting on CUDA.
  • Hardware Platform: NVIDIA GeForce MX550 (2048 MB VRAM). Peak memory consumption was strictly monitored and remained invariant at 105.52 MB (94.8% VRAM headroom).

5.2 Predeclared Model Selection Rule

Model checkpoints were selected during training using a predeclared composite validation score S combining discrimination and classification balance: S = 0.5 × ROC-AUC + 0.3 × PR-AUC + 0.2 × F1 Ties were broken by lower validation loss. Early stopping was enforced with a patience of 8 epochs without composite score improvement.

5.3 Locked Test Governance

To preserve scientific integrity and avoid test-set over-fitting, Phase D8 was designated as the locked internal evaluation. Earlier preliminary evaluation on the held-out test cohort had occurred historically during Phase C exploratory benchmarking. Upon commencement of Phase D, the entire 47-patient test cohort was placed under strict quarantine throughout Phase D1–D7 hyperparameter exploration, ablation studies, and multi-seed stability testing. No test-set labels or predictions were accessed during Phase D development or candidate selection. During Phase D8, the quarantined test cohort was unblinded for a single locked evaluation at the canonical unadjusted threshold τ = 0.50, without any post-hoc threshold adjustment or test-driven model selection. Because the internal test cohort has now been fully utilized, the test set must not be accessed for further tuning, and independent external multi-center validation is required for confirmatory assessment.

Observations: Unimodal mammography models (Exp 1 and Exp 3) suffered from severe sensitivity collapse at threshold 0.50 (detecting only 1 of 7 suspicious/actionable cases), while multimodal fusion in GIT 1 achieved balanced performance directly at threshold 0.50 (ROC-AUC 0.8857, Sensitivity 71.43%, Specificity 85.00%).

6.2 Phase C: Focal Loss Exploration & C3 Selection

Phase C explored loss modulation to address false negatives in GIT 1 on validation data (Nval = 48): - C1 (Weighted BCE Repro): S = 0.8086, Val Loss 0.4272. - C2 (Focal γ = 2.0): S = 0.8276, Val Loss 0.2537. Overfitting gap  + 0.2462. - C3 (Focal γ = 1.5): S = 0.8351, Val Loss 0.1679, Val ROC-AUC 0.9281, Val PR-AUC 0.7661, Val Sensitivity 75.00% (6/8), Val Specificity 92.50% (37/40), F1 0.7059. Healthy loss gap  + 0.0089. - C4 (Weighted BCE, Low LR): S = 0.8338, Val Loss 0.4664. - C5 (Focal, Low LR, Weight Decay 0.02): S = 0.8122, Val Loss 0.1227.

Candidate C3 was formally selected as the primary benchmark comparator based on the highest validation composite score (S = 0.8351).

6.3 Phase D1–D5: Controlled Hyperparameter Ablations

Phase D executed isolated, single-variable ablations strictly on development data: - D1 (C3 Reproduction): Bit-exact replication of C3 (S = 0.8351, Epoch 4, loss 0.1679). - D2 (Milder Focusing γ = 1.0): S = 0.8351, identical ranking, but higher loss (0.2250). - D3 (Stronger Focusing γ = 2.0): S = 0.8276, delayed convergence (Epoch 10), severe training memorization (train acc 99.55%, gap  + 0.2462). - D4 (Higher Dropout 0.40): S = 0.8334. Over-regularization caused conservative probability collapse: specificity reached 100.0%, but sensitivity collapsed to 50.00% (4/8), missing 4 suspicious lesions. - D5 (Conservative LR lr = 5 × 10 − 5): S = 0.8468 ( + 0.0117 over C3). Sensitivity increased to 87.50% (7/8,  + 1 actionable case identified: Validation True-Positive Case V1, BI-RADS 6, p = 0.5034), specificity maintained at 92.50% (37/40), F1 reached 0.7778, and validation loss reached an optimal low of 0.1390.

Candidate D5 was selected as the leading Phase D candidate strictly on validation merit.

6.4 Phase D6: Multi-Seed Stability Testing

To ensure results were not random-seed artifacts, C3 and D5 were evaluated across three predetermined seeds (42, 123, 456) on validation data (N = 48): - Sensitivity: D5 achieved 83.33% ± 7.22% vs. C3’s 75.00% ± 12.50% (lower cross-seed variance). - Specificity: D5 achieved 91.67% ± 1.44% vs. C3’s 92.50% ± 5.00% (3× lower variance). - Validation Loss: D5 achieved 0.1530 ± 0.0131 vs. C3’s 0.1813 ± 0.0553 (4× tighter stability). - Composite Score: Virtually tied: 0.8532 ± 0.0200 for D5 vs. 0.8527 ± 0.0224 for C3.

6.5 Phase D7: Threshold Operating Point & Calibration Dynamics

Phase D7 mapped operating points (τ ∈ [0.30, 0.70]) across seeds on validation data: - Asymmetric Penalty at Lower Thresholds: Lowering τ to 0.45 increased D5 sensitivity to 91.67% (+0.67 patients), but caused specificity to crash by  − 17.50% (74.17%, incurring 7 additional false alarms). The exchange ratio was over 10 false alarms for every 1 additional suspicious case triaged. - Severe Penalty at Higher Thresholds: Raising τ to 0.55 caused sensitivity to halve to 50.00%. - Selection Rule Outcome: Under three independent selection rules (canonical reference, specificity constrained  ≥ 90%, and Youden index maximization), τ = 0.50 uniquely emerged as the optimal operating threshold.

7.3 Detailed Patient Audits

  1. Discordant Case A (True Negative, BI-RADS 1):
    C3 predicted p = 0.4810 (True Negative) → D5 predicted p = 0.5240 (False Positive). A minor shift of  + 0.0430 across the 0.50 boundary caused a false alarm.
  2. Discordant Case B (True Negative, BI-RADS 2):
    C3 predicted p = 0.4539 (True Negative) → D5 predicted p = 0.5190 (False Positive). A shift of  + 0.0651 caused a false alarm.
  3. Mutual False-Negative Case C (True Suspicious, BI-RADS 5):
    Both models missed this single malignant case: C3 assigned p = 0.3001, while D5 assigned p = 0.3667. Although D5 increased the probability by  + 0.0666, it remained well below the 0.50 triage threshold.

Forensic Explanation:

  1. In Phase C, scripts/evaluate_phase_c.py computed inference dynamically for C3 and C4, but imported historical GIT 1 and GIT 2 rows via a hardcoded dictionary (lines 357–411). During composition, discrete classification counts were transcribed correctly, but continuous ranking metrics (ROC-AUC and PR-AUC) were copied from unversioned preliminary exploratory runs.
  2. The actual physical prediction CSVs from Phase 5 yield ROC-AUC = 0.8857 and PR-AUC = 0.5729 for GIT 1, and ROC-AUC = 0.8321 and PR-AUC = 0.4048 for GIT 2.
  3. Candidate C3 evaluated in Phase C matches the Phase D8 locked evaluation to full floating-point precision (100.000% agreement across all 47 predictions).
  4. No prior reports were overwritten or modified, maintaining an auditable evidentiary trail.

9. Discussion

9.1 Does Candidate D5 Demonstrate Clinical Superiority?

No. Based on locked held-out test evaluation, Candidate D5 does not surpass Candidate C3: - D5 detected zero additional cancers (6/7 sensitivity for both models). - D5 accrued two additional false positives, reducing specificity from 85.00% to 80.00% and precision from 50.00% to 42.86%. - While D5 achieved a higher composite score on validation data, this apparent advantage failed to generalize to the test cohort, exemplifying small-sample validation variance. - Consequently, Candidate C3 is reaffirmed as the primary, most balanced reference benchmark for multimodal radiologic triage in this codebase.

9.2 The Fallacy of Majority-Class Accuracy

In screening populations where low-risk cases predominate (85.11% in our test cohort), a trivial dummy classifier predicting LOW_RISK for all subjects achieves 85.11% accuracy, yet misses 100% of malignancies (Sensitivity = 0%). In contrast, Benchmark C3 achieves 85.11% accuracy while delivering 85.71% sensitivity (6 of 7 suspicious/actionable lesions identified), 85.00% specificity, and a Negative Predictive Value of 97.14%.

9.3 Statistical Power and Small-Sample Binomial Constraints

With only seven positive cancer cases in the held-out cohort, statistical power is severely constrained. The difference between C3 and D5 is statistically indistinguishable (p = 0.5000). Claims of commercial readiness or clinical superiority based on such samples are scientifically unsupportable.

10. Limitations

  1. Small Positive Sample Size (Npos = 7): The primary limitation is the small number of positive malignancies. Confidence intervals for sensitivity span over 57% ([42.13%, 99.64%]).
  2. Single-Center Retrospective Origin: BCMID originates from a single hospital in Alexandria, Egypt. Generalizability across international screening programs, diverse patient ethnicities, and varied mammographic hardware remains unestablished.
  3. Radiologic Triage vs. Histopathological Truth: Labels reflect radiologist narrative BI-RADS categories rather than universal tissue biopsy pathology.
  4. Frozen Encoders: Image encoders were frozen post-pretraining due to hardware constraints on the 2.0 GB NVIDIA GeForce MX550, leaving end-to-end multi-task backpropagation unexamined.

11. Ethical Considerations & Clinical Safety Boundary

  • Research Scope Only: This system is an automated radiologic triage research tool designed to prioritize workflow. It does NOT diagnose breast cancer, does not replace tissue biopsy, and is not approved for clinical decision-making.
  • Patient Privacy: All patient identifiers have been pseudorandomized. No unprotected health information (PHI) or identifiable facial/anatomical markers are exposed.
  • Harm of False Negatives: In oncology screening, false negatives result in delayed diagnosis. The mutual miss of the mutual false-negative case underscores why AI triage systems must serve as secondary aids under human radiologist supervision, never as autonomous gatekeepers.

12. Conclusion

This study establishes a rigorous, scientifically controlled benchmark for multimodal radiologic breast cancer triage on the BCMID dataset. Through multi-phase exploration and locked held-out testing, Candidate C3 (Class-Balanced Focal Loss γ = 1.5, lr = 10 − 4) is reaffirmed as the strongest reference model, achieving 85.71% sensitivity (6/7 suspicious/actionable cases triaged), 85.00% specificity (34/40 true negatives), 85.36% balanced accuracy, and an ROC-AUC of 0.9036 at the canonical threshold τ = 0.50.

While Candidate D5 exhibited validation gains, locked test evaluation revealed that these gains did not generalize, resulting in identical sensitivity with two additional false positives. Through transparent reporting of exact binomial confidence bounds, paired non-parametric tests, and forensic reconciliation of historical baselines, this work establishes a verifiable foundation for future multi-center prospective investigations.
